meta.title: TWENTY YEARS
meta.intro1: You are about to build a house on the outskirts of Bengaluru. Eight decisions, none of them dramatic. Every one of them is a decision real people make, for reasons that make sense at the time.
meta.intro2: You will be told what everything costs. You will not be told what anything means. When the house is finished, twenty-two years will pass — and then you will meet the person who has to open what you built.
meta.footnote: A two-floor house of about 2,000 sq ft on the Bengaluru outskirts, at roughly ₹2,250 a square foot — about ₹45 lakh. Six minutes to play. Built from field interviews with homeowners, maistries, contractors, civil engineers and architects in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

stages.title: Who will build it?
stages.scene: You've bought a 30×40 site on the outskirts of Bengaluru. Two floors, about 2,000 square feet, a budget somewhere near ₹45 lakh. Your cousin says you don't need anyone fancy — his house came up fine.

options.label: A maistry, working to your instructions
options.note: Shivanna has built four houses on this road. He will do whatever you specify, and decide whatever you don't.

options.label: A contractor, turnkey
options.note: One rate per square foot, materials and labour together. His 10–15% margin is already inside that rate, so today it costs you nothing extra.

options.label: A civil and structural engineer
options.note: Soil bearing, foundation, columns, beams, steel detailing. He can sign the plan himself.

options.label: An architect
options.note: Floor plans, elevations, plumbing and electrical layouts, full working drawings. Feels like a lot for a house this size.

stages.title: Where does the tank end up?
stages.scene: The footprint is fixed and the borewell is already sunk in the north-east. Nobody positions the tank — it takes whatever margin is left over. The vastu consultant is asked which of the leftover strips is acceptable.

options.label: The rear strip, which the consultant prefers
options.note: Leaves 0.7 m to the compound wall. Nothing can drive in. Nobody weighed that, because nobody was thinking about the tank.

options.label: The side passage, west of the kitchen
options.note: A hose could be walked in from the gate. A truck could not.

options.label: The margin along the drive
options.note: A truck can back right up to it. You lose the second parking space, and the consultant is not enthusiastic.

stages.title: What kind of tank?
stages.scene: Shivanna can quote for rings the same afternoon. Anything else needs somebody to say what they want.

options.label: Seven cement rings, ten feet deep
options.note: ₹500–850 a ring. What every house on this road has. Ready by Thursday.

options.label: One plastered brick chamber
options.note: Solid, and watertight if the plaster is done properly. Still a single compartment.

options.label: Two chambers, baffles and dip-pipes, to IS 2470
options.note: Shivanna can build this. He has done it before. It needs you to ask for it.

options.label: Leave it to Shivanna
options.note: He knows the site and he knows what people take. He will pick what he always picks.

stages.title: Finishing the yard.
stages.scene: Before you move in, the back yard is levelled and tiled. The tiler asks how you want it done along the rear. Nobody in this conversation says the word tank.

options.label: Tile straight across, level and continuous
options.note: The cleanest finish. No smell, no eyesore, nothing for children to trip over.

options.label: Leave a small inspection lid
options.note: One 300 mm square set flush with the tiles. Enough to look in.

options.label: Set two proper covers over the chambers
options.note: SFRC covers with lifting rings, ₹600–2,000 each, wide enough to put equipment down. They will be visible in the yard.

options.label: Leave it to the tiler
options.note: He will make it look finished.

stages.title: The vent.
stages.scene: A 50 mm pipe is meant to rise from the tank and carry gas away above head height. It will be visible from the road.

options.label: Leave it out
options.note: Nobody on this road has one. It isn't asked for, and the plumber doesn't carry it.

options.label: A short stub, hidden behind the plants
options.note: Technically vented. Barely above the ground, and easy to lose later.

options.label: Full vent to 2 m, with a mesh cap
options.note: You will see it from the gate.

options.label: Leave it to the plumber
options.note: He will do what he usually does.

stages.title: Where does the water go?
stages.scene: The tank overflows somewhere. Where it goes decides how long solids sit inside it — and nobody will ask you about this again.

options.label: Pipe it to the storm drain at the corner
options.note: Every house on this street already does this.

options.label: A soak pit
options.note: Standard practice. Will need clearing eventually.

options.label: Soak pit with a dispersion trench, sized for the soil
options.note: The ground here is rock and percolates slowly. This is what that soil needs.

options.label: Leave it to Shivanna
options.note: He will run it wherever the others on this road run it.

stages.title: The sanction.
stages.scene: Plan sanction comes to about ₹80,000 once labour cess and charges are counted, and takes roughly six weeks. Deviation of up to 15% can be regularised afterwards.

options.label: Build first, regularise the deviation later
options.note: Common enough on this road. You settle it when you need to.

options.label: Get the plan sanctioned
options.note: The tank will appear on the drawing as a rectangle marked 'ST'. Nothing about it will be specified, and nobody will look at it.

options.label: Sanctioned, with the tank detailed and specified
options.note: Chambers, cover, vent, invert levels — drawn, dimensioned and signed for.
options.lockNote: Nobody on your team can sign a detail. A maistry can build a compliant tank. He cannot be held accountable for one.

stages.title: Moving in.
stages.scene: The house is finished. The occupancy certificate means another round of inspections — about ₹95,000 once the regularisation is settled — and six more weeks.

options.label: Just move in
options.note: Most people on this road never applied for one.

options.label: Apply for the occupancy certificate
options.note: They will come and inspect before issuing it. They will check the rainwater harvesting.

lines: Sir, I'll do whatever you tell me. Whatever you don't tell me, I'll decide.
Tank goes wherever space is left, sir. Consultant will say which side is alright.
Rings are cheap and quick. Two-chamber costs more but it won't fill so fast. Your choice.
If we tile across it looks best. But later, opening it will be a problem.
Pipe is small money, sir. Most people say it spoils the front.
Drain connection is cheapest. Soak pit is proper, but this soil is rock.
Sanction is your side, sir. I only build.
House is ready. Come and stay.
One rate per square foot, everything included. Simpler for you.
Wherever it fits. We'll work around the consultant.
Rings are what people take. Brick if you want to spend.
Tiling across looks neatest. I'd do that.
Vent is extra work for the plumber. Your call.
Storm drain is quickest.
Sanction we can handle. It's mostly fees.
OC is a headache, honestly. Most don't bother.
I'll do the structure, and I can sign the plan myself now.
Structurally anywhere is fine. Just keep it off the footing.
I can size a proper two-chamber tank if you want one.
Code wants an access cover. Most clients ask me to hide it.
The vent should be there. IS 2470 asks for it.
Soak pit with dispersion is correct for rock.
I'll sign the plan. The tank I'll show as a box, unless you ask.
Up to you. I'll give the stability certificate either way.
I'll do full drawings — structural, MEP, sanitary, electrical.
Vastu I can work with. Access I'd think about at drawing stage.
I'd specify a proper tank. It goes into the working drawings.
I usually show a cover. Honestly, clients ask me to hide it.
The vent will show in the elevation. I can screen it.
Soak pit with dispersion — the soil here is rock, it needs it.
I sign the plan. The tank sits under my seal either way.
I'd get the OC. They check rainwater harvesting before they issue it.

items: You move in. The following summer the back yard is levelled and tiled, edge to edge. Whatever is under it is under it.
The garden goes in along the rear wall. A short pipe near the compound wall is in the way of the planting, and gets buried.
Your daughter's wedding. Two hundred people in the front yard.

Smell, and the drains running slow. The plumber finds nothing wrong with the plumbing and works out that the tank has never been emptied. An operator comes and sucks out the liquid — ₹9,000. The smell goes.
The same smell again. This time the operator tells you the bottom has gone hard and suction will not lift it. Somebody will have to get inside. It is expensive and inconvenient, and you leave it.
You cannot leave it any longer.
years.closing: In twenty-two years, nothing told you whether any of your eight decisions was a good one. At year eighteen you were told what would have to happen. You had four more years to act on it.

worker.intro: The operator arrives with one worker. He is paid for the tank, not for the hour. If the suction cannot finish the job, the second man goes in — that is understood between them before they arrive, and it is worth ₹500 to him.
worker.approachBoth: The truck cannot get past the gate, and the tiling runs unbroken across the top of the tank. The hose reaches part of the way. It is not going to be enough.
worker.approachReach: The truck cannot reach the tank. The hose is walked in from the gate and loses suction over that distance. The rest will have to be done by hand.
worker.approachSealed: There is no opening. The yard was tiled across the tank twenty-two years ago. They break through the tiles and the slab underneath — twenty minutes of work nobody is paying for. The hole is about forty centimetres across.
worker.approachSmall: The inspection lid comes up and the hose goes in. The liquid moves. The hardened layer at the bottom does not. He looks at the opening, and then he takes his shirt off.
worker.approachOpen: They lift the two covers by the rings, drop the suction line into the first chamber, and start the pump.
worker.safe1: The pump runs and the line lifts everything, because nothing in there has been sitting long enough to harden. Thirty-five minutes. They hose the covers down, set them back, and drive on to the next house.
worker.safe2: Nobody goes in. Nobody will ever know that this was a decision you made.
worker.exposure1: He goes in to the waist to break up the hardened layer by hand. There is air — the vent has been doing its work for twenty-two years — and he does not lose consciousness. He is in there for fifty minutes.
worker.exposure2: He is not injured. He will do four more tanks this week. What this does to him does not happen today, and will not be recorded anywhere as connected to this tank.
worker.collapse1: He lowers himself in. The stub vent has moved a little air over twenty-two years, but the solids have been sitting for the last eight. Four minutes in, his hands stop working properly and he cannot find the wall.
worker.collapse2: The other man gets him out.
worker.death1: Sealed for twenty-two years, unvented, and hardening at the bottom for the last eight. What is inside is not mostly air. He puts his head and shoulders through the hole.
worker.death2:
He does not call out. There is no warning and no struggle — that is the part people who have not seen it get wrong. He is unconscious before his knees are through the opening.

The other man goes in after him.

reveal.diffCaption: That is what it would have cost, while you were building, to make the tank reachable, openable and vented — {pct}% of what the house cost you. Ten dives at ₹500 would have paid for it. The desludging at year fifteen cost more than twice as much.
reveal.finding1: At no point while you were building did anything tell you a choice was wrong. Not the maistry, not the price, not the sanction, not the twenty-two years. The only number you were ever shown was money.
reveal.finding2: There were two separate chances, twenty-two years apart. A few thousand rupees at construction would have made the tank openable and vented. And even without that, emptying it every two to three years would have kept the solids moving, and nobody would ever have needed to get inside. Both were missed for the same reason: nothing in this system carries information from the person who opens the tank back to the people who built it.
leverage: Empty it every two to three years

The one thing a householder can act on tomorrow. Liquid extraction on a cycle keeps the solids mobile. Hardened sludge is what creates the need for a body in the tank, and hardening is only a function of time. IS 2470 asks for at least once in two years.

If the septic detail were a specified, signed item rather than a rectangle marked 'ST', there would be an accountable designer. A maistry can build a compliant tank. He cannot be held accountable for one.

If approval checked the disposal method and whether the tank can be opened, not only that a toilet is shown. Deviation up to 15% is regularisable, so the check has to land on what was built, not only on what was drawn.
Rainwater harvesting is already checked and GPS-tagged before the OC is issued in Bengaluru. A cleanable tank could ride the same gate.
Neither architects nor engineers are taught to design a tank for the person who will one day open it. Across this entire build, nobody mentioned him once.
reveal.credits: SANMAN · eGov Foundation. A composite scenario — not a real household or individual. Costs are indicative for the Bengaluru outskirts. Design references IS 2470 (Part 1) : 1985.
